title: Encoding Hyperuniformity in Geometric Networks: Structural Signatures and Diffusion Dynamics
authors: Yongyi Wang, Eli Newby, Yang Jiao, Salvatore Torquato, Réka Albert
abstract: Disordered hyperuniformity is a recently discovered exotic state exhibiting anomalously suppressed density fluctuations at long wavelengths, and its generalization to network systems remains an important open question. Here, we show that, across a wide range of systems, geometric networks retain substantially more long-wavelength density information from the underlying point configurations than Delaunay triangulations. Within geometric networks, hyperuniformity manifests as suppressed vertex-to-vertex fluctuations in a range of network structural observables, including closeness centrality, vertex strength, and eigenvector centrality. These measures not only distinguish hyperuniform networks from non-hyperuniform ones, but also separate near-hyperuniform configurations from hyperuniform systems with strong local disorder, solving a central challenge in network hyperuniformity. We connect these structural signatures to network dynamics by introducing a relaxation-time centrality based on diffusion and demonstrate that hyperuniform geometric networks exhibit more homogeneous relaxation behavior than non-hyperuniform geometric networks. These results reveal how the suppression of large-scale density fluctuations manifests in both network structure and diffusion dynamics.
summary: This work establishes that hyperuniformity, a state of suppressed density fluctuations, leaves distinct fingerprints on the structure and dynamics of geometric networks. By comparing these signatures to standard network representations, the authors show that hyperuniformity leads to reduced structural heterogeneity and more uniform diffusion relaxation across the network.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the exotic state of hyperuniformity, characterized by suppressed long-wavelength density fluctuations, manifests structurally and dynamically in network systems.
main_result: Geometric networks retain significantly more long-wavelength density information than Delaunay triangulations, and hyperuniformity is reflected in reduced structural heterogeneity (centrality variances) and more homogeneous diffusion relaxation behavior.
method: The authors compare geometric networks to Delaunay triangulations by analyzing structural observables (centralities) and introducing a relaxation-time centrality derived from solving the diffusion equation on the network Laplacian.
model_or_system: The study uses geometric networks constructed from various point configurations, including Poisson, Random Sequential Adsorption (RSA), and Stochastic Hyperuniformity (SHU) systems.
key_observables: Closeness centrality variance ($\sigma^2 C_{	ext{close}}$), vertex strength variance ($\sigma^2 s$), eigenvector centrality variance ($\sigma^2 C_{	ext{eig}}$), and relaxation-time centrality ($	ext{Cheat}(i)$).
important_parameters: Connection radius $R$, spatial scale $r$, and the density correlation threshold $C_0$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the spectral decomposition of the weighted Laplacian matrix for diffusion dynamics and assumes that geometric networks provide a superior representation of long-range density correlations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate geometric network constructions and compare density correlations $C(r)$ for different system types. Other figures show the scaling of the critical connection radius $R_c(r)$ and the variances of structural and diffusion metrics.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the need for better network representations than Delaunay triangulations, then quantifying the structural signatures of hyperuniformity using centrality measures, and finally connecting these structural findings to the dynamics by analyzing diffusion relaxation times.
why_interesting: The connection between macroscopic density fluctuations (hyperuniformity) and microscopic network properties (centrality, diffusion) provides a powerful, quantifiable link between continuum physics and discrete network science, relevant for understanding complex material structures.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Demonstration of geometric networks with R = 1.2 (0.012L) constructed from (A) Poisson, (B) RSA, (C) SHU (χ = 0.20), and (D) SHU (χ = 0.49) point configurations. Each point is connected to all other points within the connection radius R, as illustrated by the green circle. Although the near-hyperuniform RSA configuration exhibits stronger local order than the SHU (χ = 0.20) disordered hyperuniform systems, the latter possesses hidden long-range order. Therefore, distinguishing these systems requires a network construction that is sensitive to structural information beyond short-range local order.

Figure 2: Network density correlation C(r), as defined in Eq. 9, for (A) Delaunay triangulation networks and (B) geometric networks with connection radius R = 5 (0.05L), constructed from the point configurations considered here. The inset in (B) shows C(r) for the SHU (χ = 0.49) system as a function of spatial scale r over a range of connection radii R. The black contour denotes C0 = 0.75, and the red dashed line marks R = 5. (C) Scale dependence of the relative connection range eR(r), normalized by eR(5), as defined in Eq. 3. For all systems, eR(r) decreases with r, indicating that Rc(r) grows more slowly than the spatial scale being probed over the scales examined.

Figure 3: Variance of (A) the closeness centrality, σ2 Cclose, (B) the vertex strength, σ2 s, and (C) the eigen- vector centrality, σ2 Ceig, for geometric networks as a function of the connection radius R. Hyperuniform geometric networks exhibit suppressed variance in all three structural centrality measures. The hierarchy of the variances reflects the degree of hyperuniformity of the underlying point configurations. We note that the numerical values of different centrality measures are not directly comparable.

Figure 4: Variance of the relaxation-time central- ity, σ2 Cheat, for geometric networks as a function of the connection radius R. Similar to the structural descriptors, diffusion dynamics capture the hyper- uniform character of the underlying point configu- rations. Across the broad spectrum of systems con- sidered, hyperuniform geometric networks exhibit re- duced diffusion-relaxation heterogeneity.

Figure 5: Variance of the relaxation-time centrality, σ2 Cheat, for (A) weighted complete graphs and (B) Delaunay triangulation networks over a wide range of λ. Because geometric networks converge rapidly toward the complete-graph limit, panel A shows that the diffusion hierarchy persists in the weighted complete-graph limit. By contrast, Delaunay triangulation cannot distinguish the near-hyperuniform RSA configurations from the more locally disordered OCP and SHU χ = 0.20 systems.
